title: Chapter 53: The Net Closes, Part 2 of 5: Notches
html:
When she came out of the hay, the sun was still not up, and Wat was on deck with a knife.
He was standing at the foot of the mast in the gray half-light with his coat open and his breath smoking, and his big left hand on the wood, and the knife in it. Not cutting. Just holding it there, the point resting on the mast, about a hand's width above the boards of the deck. Waiting for her.
She stopped at the edge of the hold and looked at him.
Then she looked at the mast.
It was the mast her father had stepped, thirty years ago, when the old one cracked in the great frost. Good northern pine, straight as a ruler, tarred black at the foot where it went through the deck and oiled the rest of the way up, so that the grain showed through, gold and brown, like the side of a horse. Forty feet of it. With the yard at the top, and the red sail furled on the yard, white with frost.
And at the bottom, just above the deck, where a child could reach if it stood on its toes, the notches.
They went round the mast in a ring. Little cuts in the wood, each one no longer than the top joint of a finger. Some old, some very old, gone dark and smooth with tar and weather and hands. Some newer. Each one with letters cut beside it, small and rough, the way people carve letters who did not learn them at a school.
Hessa knew every one of them. She did not need to read them. She could not have read most of them anyway. Her mother could read. Her grandmother could not. But she knew them by where they were, the way she knew the river by its bends.
The oldest ones, low down, nearly gone, had come off the old mast, the cracked one. Her father had cut them off it with a saw, every one, in a little block of wood each, and pegged them onto the new mast in a ring, so that none of them would be lost. G.D. Her grandfather, Gil Doon. M.F. Her grandmother, Mary Fenner. And older still, below those, three blocks so worn you could only just see there had been a cut there at all. Nobody knew whose they were any more. Doons. Fenners. People who had lived on the water before the city was a city.
And above them, cut into the new mast itself, the ones she remembered being made.
J.D. Her father, Jack Doon. Cut by his own father, the year he was born, on the old mast, and carried across.
H.D. Her. Forty-one Midwinters ago. Her father had cut it with his clasp knife on the morning of her first Midwinter, the way his father had cut his, and held her up to the mast so that her hand touched it. She did not remember. She had been ten months old. But her mother had told her the story every Midwinter after, until her mother died.
C.D. Col. Wat's brother, the one who danced on tables. Cut by Wat's father, on Wat's father's barge, and when that barge sank in the Saltgate storm Col had brought the block of wood that held it to Hessa's father and asked could it go on the Grace, because the Grace was the last Doon boat left on the river. And it had.
W.D. Wat. The same.
And a space. A clean space in the ring, just to the right of W.D., where the wood was smooth and gold and untouched.
Waiting.
That was where Wat's knife was resting.
"Before the sun," said Wat. "That's the rule. Your father said."
"I know the rule."
"You do it."
She looked at him.
"You're the Doon," said Wat. "It's your boat. You do it." He held out the knife to her, handle first. "I'll hold him."
He went and got Robin.
The baby came up out of the cabin furious and sleepy and wrapped in three blankets, with his red hair sticking straight up and his face screwed shut against the cold. Wat held him in the crook of his good arm, against his chest, and the baby opened one gray eye and looked at the frost on the reeds and the gray sky and the black barge and shut it again in disgust.
Hessa took the knife.
It was Wat's sapper's knife, the one he had carried in the Foot. Short and broad and very sharp, with a horn handle worn pale. She put the point of it on the clean place on the mast, in the ring, just to the right of her husband's letters, and cut.
The wood was hard and cold, and the knife went in slowly. She cut a notch. A little short deep cut, no longer than the top joint of a finger. The way her father had done it for her. And then, beside it, small and rough, because she had only ever learned to make a few letters and these were two of them, she cut his.
R.D.
She stood back.
The new cut was very pale, almost white, against the gold of the oiled pine. Bright and raw and clean. Among all the old dark ones. Like a new star among old ones.
"Now," said Hessa.
Wat bent down, with the baby, until Robin's small fat hand in its blanket was level with the mast. And Hessa took the hand, gently, out of the blanket. It was warm and damp and very small and it tried to grab her finger. She let it. And then she took it, with her finger in it, and laid it flat against the mast. Over the new notch. Over the two rough letters.
Robin opened both eyes.
He looked at his own hand on the cold wood. And at the cut, pale under his fingers. And then he looked up, past it, up the mast, all the way up, forty feet of gold pine going up into the gray sky with the red sail at the top white with frost. His mouth fell open. He stared. Hessa did not think he had ever looked up the mast before. Not like that. Not right to the top.
He said something. Not a word. A sound. A small soft astonished sound, like a dove.
"That's yours," said Hessa Doon. "That's your place. On the Grace. With your father and me and your grandfather and his father and all of them. Whatever happens. Wherever you go. That's where you were on your first Midwinter. On the water. With us."
The baby looked at the top of the mast.
And the sun came up.
Not much of it. Just the very edge. A thin line of gold, low in the east, over the reeds, so bright after the gray that it hurt. It came across the ice in a long low flat blaze of light and hit the mast, and the gold pine lit up, all the way up, like a candle. And the frost on the red sail at the top caught fire, pink and gold. And the new notch at the bottom, pale and raw under the baby's hand, shone.
Wat made a sound in his chest. Hessa did not look at him. She knew what his face was doing. She did not want him to know she knew.
She let go of the baby's hand. Robin kept it on the mast for a moment longer by himself. Then he took it away and put it in his mouth.
And Hessa Doon stood on the deck of the Patient Grace in the first sun of Midwinter, with the knife in her hand, and thought about the girl.
The Thorne girl. Lyra. With her cropped dark hair and her set chin, who had sat on this deck on the Friday night a week ago and held her father's hand and tapped on it. Who had asked Hessa, that night, when the old lord was asleep and the harvester was getting ready to go, a question nobody had ever asked her before.
Why do you do it, Hessa? Any of it? You didn't have to. You didn't know us. Why?
And Hessa had not known what to say. She had thought about it. She had stood there with her arms crossed and thought about it for a long time, while the girl waited.
Because nobody asked me not to, she had said at last.
It was not a good answer. She knew that. But it was the true one. It was the one her father would have given, and his father. You did not leave a man in the water. You did not leave anybody in the water. That was the river. That was all the river had ever asked of anybody, in all the years before the city was a city. You pulled them out. You did not ask who they were first.
And then the Captain, Oren, on this deck, the same night, in the dusk, with the hay wain waiting on the bank to take the girl and the harvester away to the city. He had stood by the hatch and looked at her, and said, in his slow voice like a cart:
Hessa. Promise me one thing.
What?
If it comes to it. If you have to choose. Save the boy first. He had looked at the cabin, where Robin was. Robin first. Before the old lord. Before any of us. Before the boat.
And she had looked at him. At his big gray face. And she had known what it cost him to say it. Because he had carried the old lord's family for twenty-two years, and he would have died for any one of them on any day of those twenty-two years without thinking about it. And he was telling her to choose a bargeman's baby over them.
Robin first, she had said. I promise.
She looked at the new notch on the mast, bright in the first sun.
She gave Wat back his knife.
"Breakfast," she said. "And then the cake. And then we'll see about this ice."
Midwinter on the Water
They kept Midwinter on the Patient Grace the way the river people always kept it, because Hessa would not have it any other way.
Not the way the Hill kept it. Not with masks and lamps and long rooms full of people in silk, eating little cakes off silver plates. Not even the way the city kept it, the river parishes, with the three lamps in the window and the long song and the gin shops open all night. The river people had their own way. It was older. It came from before the city, Hessa's mother said, from when there was only the river and the people on it, and the river was alive, or near enough, and you had to ask it nicely to let you through the winter.
So at sunrise, when the dirty yellow line along the bottom of the sky had turned to a thin cold gold, Hessa went up on deck with a sprig of green.
She had cut it on Saturday, on the bank at Sallow Hythe, from the only tree there, an old juniper growing crooked out of the dyke. A little branch of dark green needles with pale blue berries on it, frosted white. She tied it to the top of the tiller with a piece of red wool from her own shawl. That was for the boat. So that the boat would know it was loved, and hold together till the spring.
Then she went down into the cabin and lit a candle and put it in the little square window at the back, the stern window, that looked out over the ice the way they had come. That was for anybody lost on the water. So that they could see a light, and know that somebody was waiting, and steer for it.
There was nobody lost on the water at Sedge End. There was no water. There was only ice. She lit it anyway.
And then she made the cake.
It was not much of a cake. Oats, and lard, and a handful of dried apple rings from the string that hung over the stove, and an egg, the last egg, which she had been saving since Withy Reach. And no sugar. The doctor had said no sugar, the girl had said, for the old lord, and Hessa had thought about it for a long time and decided that if the old lord could not have sugar on Midwinter then nobody on the Grace would, and that was fair. She mixed it in the old brown bowl and pressed it into the flat iron pan and set it on the top of the stove to bake slowly. The cabin filled with the smell of it. Warm oats and apple and smoke.
Wat sat on the edge of the bunk with Robin on his knee.
The baby was eleven months old. He had his mother's gray eyes and his father's red hair, a bright soft fuzz of it, like a duckling's down, that stuck straight up off the top of his head whatever you did to it. He had four teeth and was cutting a fifth, and he was not happy about it. He had chewed the corner of Wat's sleeve until it was wet through, and the edge of the blanket, and the wooden spoon, and the end of the bunk. Now he was chewing his father's thumb. Wat let him. Wat sat there with his huge red-bearded face very solemn, and his big scarred sapper's hand held out, and let his son chew on it.
"He'll have it off," said Hessa, from the stove.
"Let him."
"You'll want that thumb. For the ice."
"Got another," said Wat.
Hessa looked at them. At the big silent man and the small red-haired furious baby, in the yellow light of the stove, with the candle burning in the window behind them for nobody. She found she had stopped stirring.
She made herself start again.
It was Robin's first Midwinter. She had thought about that a lot, in the night, lying awake listening to the ice. His first. Last Midwinter he had been inside her, a hard round weight under her heart that kicked when she bent to the pole, and she had kept Midwinter at the wharf at Saltgate with her mother's sister and her husband's brothers and half the barge families of the south river, in the long shed by the lock, with a fire in a barrel and a fiddle and a sheep roasting, and Wat's brother Col had danced on the table and broken it. And she had thought, sitting there with her hands on her belly, next year he'll be here. Next year I'll hold him up to the fire and show him to everybody.
And instead here he was. At Sedge End. In the reeds. In the ice. With nobody to see him but his father and an old eel-man and a lord who did not know his own name.
She did not mind. That was the strange thing. She had thought she would. She did not.
"Wat," she said.
"Mm."
"When this is done. When the ice goes, and we take the old lord home, and the girl's got her father back, or whatever she's going to get. When it's all done." She looked at the cake in its pan. "I want to go home. To the Saltgate. To the wharf. I want to tie up by the long shed and stop there till the spring and not go anywhere."
Wat did not answer at once. He looked at the baby chewing his thumb.
"And the goat," he said.
"And the goat. I'll get Abel his goat. The best goat on the south river. A nanny, in milk. I'll tie a red ribbon on it and lead it up to the tannery door myself and say, There, Big Abel, now we're square."
Wat's red beard moved. It was the nearest he came to laughing.
"He'll not know what to do with it."
"He'll milk it," said Hessa. "Or he'll eat it. I don't care which. That's his business. Mine's to give it him."
She took the cake off the stove.
It was a little burnt on the bottom. It always was. She turned it out of the pan onto the board, and cut it into four with the big knife. One for Wat. One for her. One for the old lord, which she would soak in warm milk and feed him with the horn spoon. And one for Old Pask, the eel-man, who had nobody, and whom she would take it to on the ice when the sun was up properly.
Robin got a crust. The burnt bit from the bottom. He took it in both fists and stared at it and put it in his mouth and chewed it with his four teeth and his coming fifth, with a look of great surprise. Then he held it out to his father, very seriously, all wet, to share.
Wat took it, and ate it, wet and all.
And Hessa Doon sat down on the edge of the bunk beside them, in the warm cabin of the Patient Grace, on Midwinter morning, in the ice, at Sedge End, with the juniper on the tiller and the candle in the window, and put her arm round her husband's broad back, and her other hand on her son's soft red head, and thought that she had never been so happy in her life.
She did not say so. You did not say so, on the river. It was bad luck. The river heard you, and it remembered, and it came for what you loved, in the spring, when the ice broke.
She just sat there.
And outside, very faint, from somewhere far off across the ice, from out in the white silence among the reeds, a voice called her name.
Old Pask
It was Old Pask, coming across the ice from his hut on the rise, and he was in a hurry, and Old Pask was never in a hurry.
Hessa went up the ladder and out of the hatch and stood on the deck with her hand over her eyes against the low gold sun, and watched him come. A small bent shape, black against the white, in a coat made of a dozen old coats sewn together and a hat made of eel-skin, with the long eel-spear he always carried held out sideways in both hands for balance. He came across the ice the way the eel-men walked on it, which was not like anybody else. Flat-footed. Knees bent. Sliding more than stepping. Testing every yard in front of him with the butt of the spear before he trusted it. Tock. Slide. Tock. Slide. He had been walking on the ice of the fens for seventy winters, and he was not dead, and there were not many eel-men you could say that of.
"Hessa Doon!" he called again, when he was halfway. His voice was high and thin and cracked, like the voice of a reed when the wind blows across it. "Hessa Doon! Are you deaf, girl?"
"I'm here, Pask!"
"I know you're there. I can see you there. I'm not blind. I'm old." He came on. Tock. Slide. "Stop where you are. Don't come down on the ice. It's thin by your stern. The old channel runs there. It'll take a goose but it'll not take you."
She stopped where she was.
He came right up to the side of the barge, to the place where the ice was thickest, by the reeds, and stood there looking up at her with the low sun behind him. Close to, he was very small, and very brown, and very wrinkled, with no teeth at all and a white stubble on his chin like frost on a field, and little bright black eyes like an eel's. He smelled of eels. He always smelled of eels. He said it was the only smell a man could trust.
"Happy Midwinter, Pask," said Hessa. "I've made a cake. There's a bit for you."
"Keep your cake." He did not smile. Old Pask never smiled. He had nothing to smile with. "Listen. You listening?"
"I'm listening."
"Two men came up the dyke road from Sallow Hythe yesterday. At dusk. On horses." He jerked his chin back over his shoulder, west, toward the long low line of the dyke on the edge of the fen, a mile off, where the old road ran along the top of it from the village. "I was out at the far traps. I saw them from the reeds. They stopped on the dyke and looked out over the fen for a long time. Then they went back."
Hessa did not say anything.
"Gray coats," said Old Pask. "Long ones, with capes on the shoulders. And good horses. Too good for Sallow Hythe. Too good for anywhere round here." He spat on the ice. "And this morning I went into the Hythe for my bread, the way I do of a Monday, Midwinter or no. And the woman at the bread oven said two men in gray coats had come in yesterday and asked at every door. Was there a black barge, they said. With a red sail. Had anybody seen a black barge go north, with a red sail and a woman at the pole." He looked up at her with his little black eel's eyes. "And they'd been asking at Withy Reach the day before, the bread woman said. Her sister's at the Reach. They'd been asking all the way up."
The cold went into Hessa all at once, through her coat and her shift and her skin, right into the middle of her, the way it does when you fall through ice.
"What did they tell them?" she said. "At the Hythe?"
"They told them nothing. Nobody at the Hythe tells anybody anything. They're fen people." Old Pask spat again. "But the boy at the alehouse, the landlord's boy, the simple one, he told them he'd seen a red sail go past on Thursday. Going north. Toward the fen." He paused. "They gave him a coin. A whole silver one. He showed it to everybody. He was very proud of it."
Hessa looked out over the ice. Over the reeds, gold and gray in the low sun. Over the long low line of the dyke, a mile off, empty. Over the fen.
Forty miles of reed and channel. Every one of them looking the same. You could not find Sedge End unless you knew the way.
Unless you had a boy at the alehouse who had seen a red sail going north, toward the fen. And a dyke road that ran along the edge of it. And a pair of good horses, and all day.
And the fen had frozen.
Yesterday you could not have walked to Sedge End. You could only have come by water, by the channels, through the reeds, and you would have got lost in an hour. Today the channels were stone. Today a man could walk straight out from the dyke across the ice, a mile, in a line, toward a black barge sitting in the middle of a white field with smoke coming out of its chimney.
She looked at the chimney. At the thin gray line of smoke going straight up from the cabin into the still gold air, high, very high, higher than the reeds. You could see it for miles. She had lit the stove for the cake.
"Wat," she said, without turning round.
He was already behind her. He had come up the ladder without a sound, the way he did, with Robin in the crook of his good arm. He had heard everything. He was looking at the smoke too.
"Put the stove out," said Hessa.
Wat gave her the baby. And went back down the ladder. And she heard him, below, raking the fire out of the stove into the ash pan, and the hiss of water on coals, and then the smoke from the chimney thinning, and wavering, and going gray, and going out.
Too late, she thought. It had been going since dawn.
"How long?" she said to Old Pask.
The old eel-man looked at the sky. At the sun, low and gold in the south. At the long line of the dyke.
"If they came back to the Hythe this morning for the rest of them," he said slowly, "and if there's more of them, and if they come up the dyke road at a walk, because the road's iced and they'll not want to break a horse's leg—" He thought about it. "Noon. The bell at the Hythe rings noon. Maybe a bit after."
Hessa looked at the sun.
It was the ninth bell. Perhaps a little after. She had no bell here. There was no bell at Sedge End. But she knew the sun.
Three hours.
"Can we get her out?" she said. "The Grace. Back into the channel. South."
Old Pask looked at the ice round the barge. At the reeds frozen into it. At the long rough seam in the middle of the channel where the two edges had met in the night.
"Cut," he said. "Cut her a road. Through to the old channel by your stern, where it's thin. Two fingers, there. Then the old channel runs south a mile under the reeds before it meets the Withy. It'll be thin all the way, the old channel, because it runs. Running water freezes last." He looked at her. "Two of you, with axes. And me with the spear. A road twice her width and forty yards long." He spat. "By noon? No. By the third bell after, maybe. If your man's shoulder holds."
"His shoulder will hold."
"And then you're in a channel a barge's width, going south, at the speed of a woman with a pole, with ice on both sides of you and horses on the dyke." Old Pask shrugged. "But it's better than sitting here."
It was better than sitting here.
Hessa looked down at Robin in her arms. He had stopped chewing the crust. He was looking at Old Pask, at his eel-skin hat, with his gray eyes very wide.
"Or you could leave her," said Old Pask.
Hessa looked up.
"The Grace," said Old Pask. "Leave her. Take the old man and the babby and your man and come to my hut. And then across the fen on foot, east, the way only I know, to the Mere. There's a boat at the Mere. It's three hours' walk and you'd carry him all of it." He looked at the barge. At its black tarred sides, and its red sail furled on its yard, and the juniper tied to its tiller with red wool. "They want the boat, don't they? The black barge with the red sail. They don't know what's in it. Let them have it."
Hessa Doon stood on the deck of the Patient Grace and looked at her.
At the planks under her boots, that her grandfather had laid. At the mast, that her father had stepped. At the tiller, worn smooth and dark by three generations of hands, with a sprig of green on it, so that the boat would know it was loved.
"No," she said.
Old Pask looked at her for a long moment with his little black eyes.
"No," he said. "No, I didn't think you would. Your grandfather wouldn't have neither." He hefted his spear. "Get your axes, then, girl. I'll start at the stern."
